newsitem.title: USA: Grain prices start year with strong rally.
newsitem.headline: Grain prices start year with strong rally.

text.p: Grain prices staged a strong rally Thursday as commercial companies and speculators bought heavily on indications that demand was picking up.
In other markets, crude oil prices fell on profit-taking after recent gains.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, March wheat rose 8 cents a bushel to close at $3.89-1/4 as talk circulated on the trading floor that Egypt, a big buyer of American wheat, would soon purchase up to 500,000 metric tons.

Some traders said the business would be more likely to go to cheaper Australian or Argentine wheat. But with Sri Lanka also in the market for 100,000 tons, traders preferred to buy now and sell later.
Soybean prices also rose on talk that an influential crop consultant was soon to release a private estimate forecasting a lower-than-expected 1996 soybean crop.
January soybeans rose 8-3/4 cents a bushel to $6.99-1/4.
The Department of Agriculture will release final crop estimates for 1996 Jan. 10, with its latest estimate of the recently harvested soybean crop at 2.403 billion bushels.
But traders said Memphis, Tenn.-based Sparks Companies was rumoured to be readying a private forecast for clients Friday.
"Generally, people think that Sparks is going to have a lower bean number," said Victor Lespinasse, vice president at brokerage Dean Witter in Chicago.
Corn was buoyed by the strength in wheat and soybeans but barely eked out gains since Sparks was said to be projecting a larger-than-expected final corn crop.
March corn rose 1/4 cent to close at $2.58-1/2 per bushel.
Excellent crop-growing weather in Argentina, also a corn exporter, helped keep a lid on the corn market.

Soybean meal posted strong gains in line with soybeans but was also supported by an announcement from the Food and Drug Administration that it will ban feeding cattle any livestock feed that includes animal tissues, such as bone meal.

The move was a precaution to protect American livestock from diseases like bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), or mad cow disease. Traders said it also pointed to greater use of soybean meal as a high-protein feed supplement.
January soy meal ended at $228.60 a ton, up $2.30.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices ended lower as traders took profits from the week's gains.
February crude oil ended 23 cents lower at $25.69 a barrel and after setting a life-of-contract high of $26.05 in early trading.
"There is some position squaring after the rally, but volume is thin. The market seems hung over more than anything else," said Jeff Foose, a trader with KCS Energy in New Jersey.
February heating oil ended up 0.04 cent up at 72.11 cents a gallon, and February gasoline up 0.27 cent at 71.10 cents.
The Houston Ship Channel remained closed Thursday due to fog for a second day, delaying ships.
The channel is used by tankers to reach Houston's "Refinery Row" and by deep-draft ships to reach the Port of Houston. But traders said the closure was not dire enough to affect prices.
"It's just not a factor," said John Saucer, analyst with Smith Barney in Houston.

Continuing above-normal temperatures in the Midwest and Northeast contributed to the incentive to sell in energy markets, traders said. But freezing weather in Europe was underpinning fuel prices on both sides of the Atlantic.
February natural gas futures at NYMEX ended 13.3 cents higher at $2.89 per million British thermal units.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, lumber prices rallied as traders returned from the holidays. January lumber closed up $18.80 at $443.50 per thousand board feet.
"Some (buyers) are coming back to the market that have been out of the market for two or three weeks," said Neil Schmaedick, Smith Barney Forest Products analyst.
Wholesalers and dealers were short of lumber while production was still minimal due to the holidays and poor weather in the Northwest, traders said.
